title: Painting and Compositing
description: Understand the paint and composite stages of the rendering pipeline, how layers are created, and how to use CSS to keep animations off the main thread.

data.text: After layout calculates element geometry, the browser must paint pixels and composite layers. Paint is expensive because it involves rasterizing text, shadows, borders, and images. Compositing is cheaper because it only assembles already-painted layers. The key to smooth animations is doing as much work as possible in the compositor stage.

Painting is the process of turning vector and text instructions into pixel bitmaps. Each element that needs visual rendering must be painted into one or more bitmaps. Paint is expensive because it touches every pixel, especially for large elements, blur effects, and complex backgrounds.

data.title: What Triggers Paint
data.content: CSS properties that require a paint pass.

data.text: The compositor assembles painted layers into the final image. Each layer is a bitmap that can be moved, scaled, or faded independently. Because compositing runs on a separate compositor thread, animations that only change layer transforms or opacity never block the main thread.

data.title: Creating a Compositor Layer
data.content: How browsers decide to create layers and how you can influence it.

data.text: An animation is cheap if it only touches compositor-only properties: transform and opacity. Any other animated property — width, height, left, top, margin — triggers layout or paint on every frame, which blocks the main thread and causes jank.
Even when you cannot avoid paint, you can reduce its cost. Avoid large painted areas, reduce the frequency of paint, and use containment to tell the browser what does not change.

data.title: CSS Containment and Paint Reduction
data.content: Use CSS containment to limit paint scope and improve performance.

data.text: When using React animation libraries, ensure they animate transform and opacity. Framer Motion, React Spring, and AutoAnimate all default to these properties. Avoid layout-triggering animations such as animating height from auto or top/left directly.

data.title: React Animation Best Practices
data.content: Write React animations that stay on the compositor.

data.title: Layer Explosion
data.text: Every promoted layer consumes GPU memory. Promoting hundreds of elements will exhaust memory and cause the browser to collapse layers, leading to sudden performance cliffs. Use DevTools Layers panel to audit your layer count and remove unnecessary promotions.

terms.definition: The process of rasterizing elements into pixel bitmaps; expensive because it touches many pixels.
Assembling already-painted layers into the final screen image; cheap and often GPU-accelerated.
Promoting an element to its own compositor layer so its transforms and opacity can be animated independently of the main thread.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Paint rasterizes pixels; compositing assembles layers — compositing is much cheaper
Transform and opacity are compositor-only properties and safe for 60fps animations
Animating width, height, top, left, or margin triggers layout and paint on every frame
Layer promotion via will-change or 3D transforms moves work to the compositor thread
Too many layers exhaust GPU memory and can cause sudden performance cliffs
CSS containment and content-visibility reduce paint scope
Inspect layer count in Chrome DevTools Layers panel
data.takeaway: The fastest paint is the one you avoid. Keep animations on compositor-only properties, promote layers sparingly, and use containment to shrink the painted area.
